units.t: The 20th Century. Episode one.
In this episode: The Christmas Truce of 1914, The Great Depression and Dunkirk: the miracle of 1940.
Part one. The Christmas Truce of 1914.
Five months into the most industrial war yet fought, enemy soldiers climbed out of their trenches, shook hands and sang carols together.
Then they went back to killing each other.
Live and let live.
In August 1914 many expected the war to be over by Christmas.
Instead, the German advance was stopped at the Marne and both armies dug in.
By winter trenches ran from the Belgian coast to the Swiss border, sometimes only fifty to a few hundred metres apart.
Men lived in freezing water among rats and the unburied dead.
Yet the closeness let them hear the enemy talking, coughing and singing.
Small unofficial understandings grew.
Each side might spare the other at breakfast, or let men fetch water or bring in wounded.
Historians call it ‘live and let live’.
In December Pope Benedict XV called for a Christmas pause, but governments ignored him.
Candles on the parapet.
On Christmas Eve 1914, British soldiers in several sectors were astonished to see lights along the German trenches.
German troops had placed small Christmas trees, decorated with candles, on their parapets.
Then came singing, including ‘Stille Nacht’, Silent Night.
The British replied with their own carols, and each side applauded the other across no man's land.
Shouted conversations followed, helped by Germans who had worked in Britain and spoke English.
A few brave men walked out unarmed.
When nobody fired, others followed.
By Christmas morning, along stretches of the front, men who had been trying to kill each other days earlier stood together in the frozen mud.
Gifts, graves and football.
Letters home describe an extraordinary day.
Men exchanged cigarettes, chocolate, plum puddings, buttons and badges, and showed each other photographs of their families.
Barbers cut enemy hair.
Most importantly, both sides used the calm to recover and bury the bodies lying between the lines, sometimes with joint services.
Football is the most famous part of the story.
Several soldiers wrote of kickabouts with the enemy, sometimes with a makeshift ball, and these accounts seem genuine.
But a single organised match with a final score is much harder to prove.
Historians think informal games happened in a few places, not one grand fixture across the front.
Not everywhere, not for everyone.
It is easy to imagine the whole front falling silent, but that did not happen.
The truce was strongest where British and German troops faced each other, especially around Ypres in Belgium.
It occurred in some French and Belgian sectors too, but less often, perhaps because those soldiers were fighting on their own invaded soil.
Elsewhere fighting continued and men were killed on Christmas Day.
Some truces lasted only hours, others until New Year or beyond.
By some estimates around one hundred thousand soldiers took part, but nobody knows the true figure.
Many soldiers felt uneasy, some officers were furious, and not every man who wrote home that week described peace.
Never again.
High commands saw the truce as a threat to discipline.
If soldiers came to like their enemies, how could they be ordered to kill them?
In following years strict orders forbade fraternisation, and bombardments were sometimes scheduled for Christmas.
Small local pauses still happened in 1915, but nothing like 1914.
The war grew more brutal, with poison gas, the Somme and Verdun.
When British newspapers printed soldiers' letters and photographs in January 1915, readers were amazed.
Some retellings are romanticised, but the core is well documented in hundreds of letters and diaries.
The truce did not shorten the war.
Its power lies in an uncomfortable question: if the men in the trenches could stop, why couldn't those in charge?
The key idea: Soldiers in trenches only metres apart began informal understandings to hold fire, which made the Christmas truce possible.
Part two. The Great Depression.
In 1929 the world economy began to collapse.
By the early 1930s, a quarter or more of workers in countries like the US and Australia had no job, and the politics of the decade turned dark.
Boom, then crash.
After World War I, the United States boomed.
Cars, radios and electric appliances spread into homes, often bought on instalment plans, and share prices soared.
Many people bought shares 'on margin', paying a small deposit and borrowing the rest, betting prices would keep rising.
A modest fall can wipe out the buyer's whole stake.
On 'Black Tuesday', 29 October 1929, panic selling hit the New York Stock Exchange and brokers demanded margin loans be repaid.
By mid-1932 the market had lost about 89% of its peak value, and it did not regain that peak until 1954.
But the crash alone didn't cause the Depression.
It began a wider collapse in spending, lending and confidence.
Banks fail, soil blows.
Frightened depositors rushed to withdraw savings, and around 9,000 American banks failed between 1930 and 1933, with no deposit insurance to protect savers.
Businesses cut production and workers, so people had less to spend, which led to more cuts: a vicious circle economists call a deflationary spiral.
Falling prices made debts harder to repay.
By 1933 about a quarter of American workers had no job, and shanty towns nicknamed 'Hoovervilles' after President Herbert Hoover appeared on city edges.
Nature added to the misery.
Farmers on the southern Great Plains had ploughed up millions of hectares of native grassland for wheat.
When severe drought struck in the early 1930s, the bare topsoil blew away in huge dust storms.
Hundreds of thousands left, many heading to California, a story told in Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath.
Australia in the Depression.
The collapse spread through trade and finance.
American lenders called in loans, and countries raised tariffs, like the US Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930.
World trade shrank by about two-thirds in value between 1929 and 1934.
Australia, dependent on wool and wheat exports and on borrowing from London, suffered badly.
Unemployment peaked near 30% in 1932, among the highest in the developed world.
Governments argued over whether to cut spending to keep repaying London loans.
The 1931 Premiers' Plan cut wages, pensions and public spending.
NSW Premier Jack Lang refused to pay British bondholders, and in 1932 the governor dismissed him.
The unemployed got food relief called 'the susso', often in return for work, and many men went 'on the track' with a swag, looking for jobs.
The response.
At first, many governments cut spending to balance budgets, which most economists now believe made things worse.
In 1933, US President Franklin D.
Roosevelt launched the New Deal: public works that built roads, dams and schools, bank reforms, federal deposit insurance and, in 1935, social security for older people.
Economist John Maynard Keynes argued, most famously in his 1936 General Theory, that governments should spend more during downturns to boost demand.
Leaving the gold standard also helped countries recover by freeing them to lower interest rates.
Recovery was slow, and full employment returned in many countries only with rearmament for World War II.
Lasting lessons.

Mass unemployment and despair helped extremist movements, most catastrophically in Germany, where the Nazi Party's vote surged from under 3% in 1928 to about 37% in July 1932 as the economy collapsed.
The Depression also shaped economics for generations.
Deposit insurance, unemployment benefits, central banks acting as lenders of last resort, and government stimulus during recessions all grew from its lessons.
They were used again in the 2008 global financial crisis, when Australia paid cash stimulus to households, and in the 2020 pandemic, with JobKeeper wage subsidies.
Economic hardship can reshape politics, not just household budgets.
The key idea: The 1920s boom rested on borrowing, and the 1929 crash began a wider collapse in spending and confidence.
Part three. Dunkirk: the miracle of 1940.
In nine days in 1940, an army that seemed doomed was carried home across the English Channel.
Britain called it a miracle.
Churchill warned that wars are not won by evacuations.
Trapped, then a pause.
On 10 May 1940 Germany attacked the Netherlands, Belgium and France.
Allied commanders sent their best troops, including most of the British Expeditionary Force, north into Belgium.
But German tanks came through the hilly Ardennes, which the French thought too difficult for armour, crossed the Meuse and reached the Channel on 20 May.
Hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers were caught in a shrinking pocket.
On 24 May the German advance halted, confirmed by Hitler.
Tank maintenance, marshy ground, fear of counterattack and Göring's claim that the Luftwaffe could finish the job may all have played a part.
The pause lasted around three days, giving the Allies time to strengthen the perimeter, where French troops held out.
Operation Dynamo.
Vice-Admiral Bertram Ramsay organised the rescue from rooms deep in the cliffs below Dover Castle.
The codename, Operation Dynamo, is said to come from a room that once housed an electrical generator.
When it began on 26 May, planners hoped to save perhaps 45,000 men in two days.
Conditions were terrible.
Bombing had wrecked Dunkirk's docks, oil tanks burned and black smoke hung over the town.
The beaches sloped so gently that large ships could not get close.
Men waited for days on the sand under air attack, in long lines into the sea.
Ramsay's staff worked almost without sleep, improvising hour by hour.
Mole and little ships.
The famous image of Dunkirk is a flotilla of pleasure boats, fishing vessels and yachts crossing the Channel.
These ‘little ships’ were real and heroic, many crewed by naval reservists or their owners, and vital for carrying men from the shallow beaches to larger ships offshore.
But most soldiers were taken off from the East Mole, a long concrete and timber breakwater protecting the harbour.
It was never designed for ships to tie up against, yet destroyers and passenger ferries came alongside and loaded thousands of men at a time.
Many hundreds of vessels took part, from warships to Thames barges.
The Royal Navy's destroyers did the heaviest lifting, and several were sunk.
Fighting overhead and behind.
Soldiers on the beaches were bombed and strafed, and many angrily asked where the Royal Air Force was.
In fact the RAF was flying hard, but much of its fighting took place inland or above the cloud, intercepting bombers before they reached the coast.
It lost many aircraft and pilots.
On the ground, defending the perimeter mattered just as much.
British units fought delaying actions, and French troops held the line until the end, letting others escape.
When the evacuation finished on 4 June, tens of thousands of French soldiers who had protected the beaches were left behind and taken prisoner.
Their sacrifice is often forgotten in the British telling.
A defeat remembered as victory.
Around 338,000 Allied soldiers were carried to England, including well over 100,000 French troops, many quickly shipped back to fight in France.
Against the original hope of 45,000, it seemed a miracle.
But many ships were sunk, and the British army abandoned almost all its heavy equipment: tens of thousands of vehicles, hundreds of tanks, guns and ammunition.
France signed an armistice on 22 June.
Yet Britain kept the core of a trained army, later the backbone of forces in Africa, Italy and Normandy.
On 4 June Churchill told the Commons that wars are not won by evacuations and called the campaign a colossal military disaster.
He ended with his promise to fight on the beaches and never surrender.
The key idea: A fast German breakthrough trapped the Allied armies against the sea, and a three-day halt order gave them time to defend Dunkirk.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was the ‘live and let live’ system?
Answer. Informal habits of holding fire on quiet sectors.
Question two. Why can buying shares 'on margin' be so risky?
Answer. A small price fall can wipe out the stake.
Question three. Why were the Allied armies caught in a pocket near Dunkirk?
Answer. German tanks broke through where least expected.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
